qa.name: Popliteus
qa.origin: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle (via a strong tendon inside the knee joint capsule); lateral meniscus
qa.insertion: Posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line
qa.function: Unlocks the fully extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia (or medially rotating the tibia) — initiates knee flexion from full extension; stabilises the posterior knee capsule
qa.clinical_note: Popliteus is described as the key that unlocks the knee — the fully extended knee is in a close-packed (screw-home) position with the tibia externally rotated. Popliteus initiates flexion by medially rotating the tibia (or laterally rotating the femur on the fixed foot). Its tendon passes inside the knee capsule and attaches to the lateral meniscus — it retracts the lateral meniscus during knee flexion, preventing impingement. Popliteus tendinopathy causes posterolateral knee pain, particularly on downhill running.

qa.name: Tibialis Posterior
qa.origin: Posterior surface of the interosseous membrane, adjacent tibia and fibula
qa.insertion: Tuberosity of navicular (primary); slips to all cuneiforms, cuboid, and bases of metatarsals 2–4
qa.function: Inverts the foot (primary invertor); plantarflexes the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch of the foot
qa.clinical_note: Tibialis Posterior is the deepest and most central muscle of the deep posterior compartment. Its tendon passes posterior to the medial malleolus in the tarsal tunnel. Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction (TPTD) is the most common cause of adult-acquired flatfoot deformity — progressive tendon degeneration leads to loss of the medial arch, hindfoot valgus, and forefoot abduction. It is assessed clinically by the single-heel-rise test. L4 root involvement affects both tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior (both inversion).

qa.name: Flexor Digitorum Longus
qa.origin: Posterior surface of the middle three-fifths of the tibia, medial to the vertical line
qa.insertion: Bases of the distal phalanges of the lateral four toes
qa.innervation: Tibial nerve (L5, S1, S2); flexes lateral four toes
qa.function: Flexes the lateral four toes (all joints); plantarflexes the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch; grips the ground during walking
qa.clinical_note: FDL passes posterior to the medial malleolus in the tarsal tunnel — remember Tom, Dick and Harry (Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery/nerve, flexor Hallucis longus) from anterior to posterior in the tarsal tunnel. In the sole of the foot FDL crosses over FHL (the knot of Henry) — a surgical landmark. FDL is used for tendon transfer in tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction to reconstruct the medial arch (FDL transfer procedure).

qa.name: Flexor Hallucis Longus
qa.origin: Posterior surface of the lower two-thirds of the fibula and interosseous membrane
qa.insertion: Base of the distal phalanx of the great toe (plantar surface)
qa.innervation: Tibial nerve (L5, S1, S2); flexes great toe — push-off muscle
qa.function: Flexes all joints of the great toe; plantarflexes the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch; provides the final push-off in the gait cycle
qa.clinical_note: FHL is the most powerful of the deep posterior compartment muscles despite being the most laterally placed — it is the main push-off muscle for the great toe in walking and running. Its tendon passes posterior to the medial malleolus (last in Tom, Dick and Harry — the Harry), then through a fibro-osseous tunnel beneath the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus. FHL tendinopathy (dancer's tendinopathy) is a classic overuse injury in ballet dancers from repetitive plantarflexion en pointe. Trigger toe (stenosing tenosynovitis of FHL) causes great toe catching or locking.
